name: Behemoth

facts.text: NPC pass (HEROES.md decision 11): Father Kenelm has the clerics he trains read Job's verse on the Behemoth before they go down; Pico keeps the imps' book on its death at its stall. Living Server writing.

facts.text: Until April 2002 Legion summoned Behemoth from elsewhere in the dungeon; Mythic then kept it to its own area.
Level 99, 600,000 health, partnered with Legion in the catalog, on a ledge above Legion's lair (249: 44490, 49588, 20833). No scripted mechanic beyond its reset.
2002 comments describe it one-shotting players during Legion raids; a 2009 Grab Bag answer (post-period) said it cannot be killed.

Behemoth: NPC template 60158340 (level 99), 600,000 health, GetResist 40 melee / 70 other, AF 550, absorb 50%, CC immune, aggro range 500; its OnAttackEnemy kills the target of every attack it makes, whatever the result.
The Behemoth was in the hollow before the court, was at the Feast and neither knelt nor was eaten, and is on no Roll (neutral history).
The Master's look at the Feast, the Door-Book's single line and its second line, Sir Cadfan Hir's eighty and the imps' book are Living Server writing.
Real-world myth, not game canon: in the Book of Job (40:15-24) God shows Job Behemoth, 'the chief of the ways of God', whose bones are like bars of iron.

The book pages after the first (the Chancellor's margin, Bardi Tofason's tale) and the chapter 'Under the Heading of Weather' (the Archivist's column of breaths, the examiner of the Second Roll, the shorter breaths of the Tenth Roll) are Living Server writing.

story:
Every account of the hollow agrees that the Behemoth was there first, before the lords, in the Uncounted Age; the Inquisitors say the hollow is only the shape it left when it lay down. It is not a demon, does not speak or bargain or eat souls, and is on no Roll; the Chancellor has never written its name. The Church reads it in Job, the beast of God's first making whom only its maker can approach with a sword; the skalds say it is one of the old ones from before the gods; the druids, a hill that has not yet decided to lie still. The Door-Book kept at the castle ruins gives it one line: the beast on the ledge.

It lay along the wall of the deepest chamber at the Feast of Thrones. It did not fight or kneel, and when the Master had eaten nineteen lords he looked at it, and it looked back, and he did not try to eat it. The Inquisitors say the bargain is about place and the beast has none; the imps say the Master was afraid. It lies now on a ledge above his lair, breathing like a forge, kept as a man keeps a chained bear.

It does not need to strike well, only to strike: whatever it swings at it ends, shield or mail or quick feet, landed or not. It is slow to notice anyone not close to its nose. Its hide turns blades and drinks spells. Once the Master called it down, and it did not stop at the enemy, and it went back to its ledge by itself.

Sir Cadfan Hir of Camelot Hills, who had killed the Master once, took eighty on to the ledge to see what the Master feared. The beast lifted its head and Cadfan was gone; his company sent a fresh man in front of it all night, and the Door-Book's list of their names fills a leaf. The imps take any odds against its death and have never paid. The Door-Book's last line: do not count it. Count your own and go home.
legend: The Behemoth is certain death, beyond even the whole muster of any realm, and it takes as much killing as three hundred raiders. No charm or stun holds it, its hide is as good as the finest armour and swallows half of every blow, and on top of that four-tenths of every weapon stroke and seven-tenths of everything else are lost on it. Every swing it takes kills whatever it swings at, outright: hit, miss, parry, block or dodge all end the same way, so no shield-bearer survives it and shields or dodging do nothing. It sits on the ledge above Legion's lair and only notices you within about seventeen paces, so it is easy to leave alone, and that is the advice. Here it does not come down to help Legion. If you insist on trying it, the only theory is a line of throwaway bodies to stand in front of it, one per swing, while everyone else wears down three hundred raiders' worth of killing at those odds: nobody here has done it, nobody has tried it, and the imps will take your money. Break off the fight for 8 seconds and it is whole again.

loremasterTopic.text: On a ledge above [Legion]'s lair in [Darkness Falls] lies a beast older than the court and on no Roll. It was at the Feast of Thrones and the Master did not try to eat it. Whatever it swings at, it ends, landed or not. The Church forbids Albion's companies the ledge. I would add my voice.

bookPage: From the Door-Book of the castle ruins, under the heading of things in the hollow that the companies should not count. The beast on the ledge. Sir Cadfan Hir took eighty on to it, in the season after Sir Aldous Fenn broke the Master, to learn what the Master was afraid of. The beast lifted its head and Cadfan was not there any more. Whatever it swings at, it ends; it makes no difference whether the swing lands. They fought it all night, a fresh man in front of it whenever the last was gone. At dawn they came down and it lay down. Below, in another ink: do not count it. Count your own and go home.

Not entered. Adremal wrote those two words in the margin of the First Roll, beside the space where the beast would have stood if it stood anywhere, and he has copied the margin faithfully onto every Roll since, down to the Tenth. The Archivist once asked why a chancellor who writes everything should leave a gap. The answer is kept in the Archivist's own hand. A Roll is a list of those who may fall, the Chancellor said, and a thing that cannot fall cannot be listed. To write its name would be to promise the Master that one day he might eat it, and I do not make promises on his behalf that I cannot keep. The Archivist entered the answer under the heading of law, and then, after some thought, under the heading of weather.

Bardi was the name of a man, the son of Tofi of the Vale of Mularn. He was a thane and well liked, and quick to take up a dare. Bardi went down through the snow door in a summer when Midgard held the frontier, with three bands of the best men of Mularn and Audliten, and he said he would see the beast on the ledge with his own eyes. Of what was done on the ledge nothing is told. Bardi came up alone in the morning, without his shield. His kinsmen asked him how it had gone, and he said: it looked back. They asked him about the men of the three bands, and he said the same. He lived nine winters after that and gave the same answer to every question touching the hollow, and to no other question. Here ends the tale of Bardi Tofason.

chapters.title: Before the Count
chapters.text:
Every account of the hollow, the court's and the three realms', agrees on one thing and on almost nothing else: the Behemoth was there first.

The court calls the age before the Feast of Thrones the Uncounted Age, because nobody kept a count of anything, least of all of the dead, and the court's chroniclers, who will lie about any point touching their own dignity, do not lie about this. The Behemoth was in the hollow before there were lords in it. It was there before there was a hollow, the Inquisitors say, and the hollow is only the shape it left when it lay down. The court has no word for what it is. It is not a demon. It does not speak, or bargain, or eat souls; it is not on any Roll, and the Chancellor, who writes everything, has never written its name.

The realms name it from their oldest books. The Church of Camelot reads it in Job, where God shows the man of Uz the beast called Behemoth, whose bones are bars of iron and whose strength is in his loins, the first of the ways of God, which only his maker can approach with a sword. The priests say the court has a creature of God's first making chained above its lowest door, and that this is the court's greatest blasphemy; Father Kenelm of Caer Gothwaite has every cleric he trains read the verse aloud before they go down. The Midgard skalds say it is one of the old ones that were before the gods, the frost-born kind, left behind in the dark when the world was made from the rest. The druids of Tir na Nog say it is not a beast at all but a hill that has not yet decided to lie still.

The Door-Book of the castle ruins does not try to say what it is. It has a single line on the Behemoth, written in the first season, under the heading of things in the hollow that the companies should not count: the beast on the ledge.

chapters.title: At the Feast
chapters.text:
The Behemoth was at the Feast of Thrones, and that is the strangest thing in the court's whole history.

The court says it was lying along the wall of the deepest chamber when the thirty lords came in, as it had lain there since the Uncounted Age began, and that the lords walked round it as men walk round a boulder in a field. The twenty-nine fought. The hungry one ate. The Behemoth did not move. When the eleven knelt, it did not kneel. When the Master had eaten nineteen lords and their voices were speaking out of his single throat, he turned, the court says, and looked at the beast along the wall, and the beast looked back, and the Master did not try to eat it.

Nobody below says why. The Inquisitors say the bargain of the Feast is about place, and the Behemoth has no place, so the bargain does not touch it. The Chthonic Knights say the Master was full. The imps, who have never been afraid to say anything about anyone so long as they are far enough away, say the Master was afraid, and that a court whose first law is that its king may eat anyone who falls has, lying along the wall of its deepest room, the one thing in the world that its king will not try to eat.

After the Feast the court moved the Behemoth, or the Behemoth moved itself; the accounts differ. It lies now on a ledge above the Master's lair, at the bottom of the long slope where the Rolls are cut, and it breathes there like a forge. The court keeps it as a man keeps a chained bear, the imps say: for show, and for fear, and because nobody has the courage to unchain it. The Chancellor's clerks, who will not write its name, walk past the ledge with their eyes on the Rolls.

chapters.title: What It Swings At
chapters.text:
The Behemoth does not fight as anything else in the hollow fights. It does not need to strike well. It needs only to strike.

That is how the companies of all three realms tell it, and the court says the same. A blow from the beast on the ledge is not turned by a shield, the Midgard bands say, nor slipped by a quick man, nor softened by the best mail of Jordheim; whatever it swings at, it ends, and it makes no difference whether the swing lands. The Church of Camelot says this is the meaning of Job's verse, that only its maker can approach it with a sword. The druids say a hill does not need to aim when it falls. The warden of the castle ruins wrote that every company which went up on the ledge and came down again came down without anyone who had stood in front of it.

It is not quick to wake. It lies on its ledge and breathes, and lets the companies of the realms pass below it on their way to the Master's door, and does not seem to see them. Only a man who comes up close, the imps say, a few strides from its nose, has ever been noticed. The court's own demons do not go up on the ledge at all. Its hide is harder than anything the realms' smiths can shape, the companies say; their spells sink into it and their blades turn half their weight away, and the mark a whole company can leave on it in a night is not a mark that anyone has thought worth describing.

Once, the imps say, the Master called it down to fight beside him, and it came down, and did not stop at the enemy. That story belongs to the Master. What belongs to the Behemoth is the end of it: that it went back up to its ledge by itself, and lay down again, and has not come down since.

chapters.title: Under the Heading of Weather
chapters.text:
The court keeps no Roll for the Behemoth, but it keeps a record of it all the same, and the record is the Archivist's. In his record room below the long slope he keeps the court's weather: the heat that comes up out of the deep places, the damp of the north-west where the worm lies under the chapter house, the cold that never leaves Baelerdoth's hall, the soot in the air after a high lord has lost his temper. Among these, in a column of its own, he keeps the breathing of the beast on the ledge. The Chancellor ruled on the First Roll that a thing which cannot fall cannot be listed, and the Archivist found that a thing which cannot be listed can still be measured.

He measures it as the fishermen of the realms measure a tide: so many breaths between one of the court's hours and the next, so much warmth in the stones of the slope below the ledge, the colour of the soot on the rock above it. The column runs unbroken from the First Roll to the Tenth, the imps say, except for a single night. For that night the Archivist wrote no breaths at all, and beside the empty space, in his small hand: the ledge is empty; the Master has called it down. The line after is the next night, and the breathing is as it always was, and nothing in the column says how the beast came back up, because the Archivist does not write down what he did not measure.

The Inquisitors of the north tried once to do better. In the Second Roll, the court says, they sent an examiner up the slope to put to the beast the question they put to every visitor below: whom do you serve? He was young in his office and careful in it. He carried his tablet and his stylus and went up in the proper form, and he stopped, as the law of examination requires, a long stride from the one examined. That was close enough to its nose. The tablet came back down the slope by itself, the imps say, skidding on the stones, with the question on it in his hand and nothing written under it. The Inquisitors entered the answer as irregular and, by the law of portions, referred it to Prince Ba'alorien, who sent it back unread with a note that he did not eat weather.

The column has changed only once since then, and the court argues over what the change means. In the Tenth Roll, when the three doors opened and the companies of the realms began to come down, the breaths grew shorter. Not by many: the Archivist counts a handful more to the hour than he counted through the long feuds. The Chancellor says the beast is old. The Chamberlain, who keeps the empty chair, says it is listening for something. The imps have opened a book on what it is listening for, and they say that so far nobody, mortal or demon, has been willing to take the other side.

chapters.title: Those Who Went Up
chapters.text:
Every realm has a company that went up on the ledge, and none of them has a song that ends well.

Albion's is in the Door-Book. It was the company of Sir Cadfan Hir of Camelot Hills, a knight who had killed the Master once and wanted, he said, to know what the Master was afraid of. He took eighty up the long slope and past the Master's door and on to the ledge, in the season after Sir Aldous Fenn broke the Master, and he went up first, with his shield. The warden recorded what the survivors told him. The beast lifted its head. Cadfan was not there any more. The company fought it for most of a night, sending a fresh man to stand in front of it whenever the last one was gone, and the warden's list of their names fills a whole leaf. At dawn they came down. The beast lay down. Of its wounds, the survivors said nothing.

Midgard's skalds tell of a thane who went up with three bands and came down alone, and who answered every question about it afterwards with the same three words. Hibernia's bards sing of a champion who went up with no shield at all, as no champion of the old songs ever did, on the reasoning that a shield would make no difference, and they sing that the reasoning was sound.

The imps keep a book on it, as they keep a book on everything. Any imp of the three halls will take a seal against the Behemoth's death, at any odds the buyer likes, and Pico, who keeps that book at its stall in the Albion hall, says they have never yet paid out. The Church forbids Albion's companies to go up on the ledge. The warden's last word on the beast, under the single line of the first season, is a second line, added in another ink: it is not a thing to be counted. Do not count it. Count your own and go home.
